1. INTRODUCTION 
The fast proliferation of edge-enabled embedded 
systems 
has 
fundamentally 
changed 
the 
data 
processing 
paradigm 
in 
smart 
sensing 
systems, 
wearable health systems, autonomous control systems, 
and industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). With all this, 
edge 
computing 
drastically 
reduces 
end-to-end 
latency, eliminates network congestion, and minimizes 
reliance on cloud computing systems [1], [2]. To a 
more specific extent, these benefits are vital to 
latency-sensitive and privacy-conscious applications. 
But edge devices are usually subject to strong energy 
consumption, silicon area, and computational resource 
limits, and optimization of hardware at the hardware 
level, is a primary design requirement. One of the 
essential issues in embedded VLSI systems has 
continued to be energy efficiency particularly battery 
powered and energy-harvesting devices used in remote 
or 
inaccessible 
locations 
[3]. 
Simultaneously, 
expanding connectivity and physical access to edge 
devices makes them vulnerable to a broad scope of 
security threats, such as the firmware manipulation, 
unauthorized access, cloning, and physical intrusions 
[4]. In such a case, software-only security solutions are 
frequently not sufficient because they are weak to 
low-level attacks, and they incur extra overhead in 
terms of performance and power consumption. This 
has further motivated the use of security mechanisms 
aided by hardware, i.e. secure boot, hardware root of 
trust 
and 
cryptographic 
accelerator 
as 
critical 
elements in trustworthy embedded platforms [5], [6]. 
ABSTRACT 
Embedded systems with edges are critical in the new applications in the Internet of 
Things 
(IoT), 
smart 
healthcare, 
industrial 
automation 
and, 
cyber 
physical 
infrastructures. Such systems need to be under strict energy requirements and, at the 
same time, be highly resistant to tampering with their firmwares, unauthorized access, 
and physical attacks. Nevertheless, the majority of VLSI architectures have methods to 
discuss energy efficiency and security as orthogonal design constraints, resulting in 
inefficient trade-offs and higher overheads when implemented in resource-constrained 
edge conditions. The current paper suggests a safe and power efficient VLSI design that 
is directly aimed at edge-driven embedded systems. This proposal follows the principle 
of unified co-design that can be utilized to integrate lightweight hardware security 
primitives such as a hardware root of trust, secure boot mechanism, cryptographic 
acceleration with multi-level energy optimization methods, such as dynamic voltage 
and frequency scaling (DVFS), fine-grained clock gating, and power gating. A design 
methodology based on register-transfer level (RTL) is used to describe the architecture 
and it is implemented in industry-standard synthesis tools to make it practically 
feasible. A detailed analysis of the proposed design with realistic edge workloads 
proves that the design significantly reduces the overall energy consumption and the 
energy per operation relative to a nominal embedded architecture with only a low 
overhead in the area and performance. Moreover, the internal security provisions offer 
a high level of protection against high firmware-based and communication threats 
without negating energy high efficiency. The findings validate that security and power 
co-optimization in architectural settings is an effective and required process of the 
next-generation edge computing platforms. The proposed VLSI architecture will come 
up with a secure, scalable, and low-energy solution to low-latency and low-power edge 
intelligence applications.

Most of the existing works discussed the energy 
optimization and security as design objectives even 
though the design of a low-power-based VLSI and a 
secure embedded architecture has been studied 
extensively. Power-efficient architectures do not put 
security into consideration and secure processor

are often added as post-design additions instead of 
being co-designed with power management, and it 
results in an inefficient trade-off into the aptness of 
resource-constrained edge environments. This points 
at a critical research void, namely the absence of an 
integrated VLSI architecture that becomes optimized 
in terms of energy efficiency and hardware-level 
security of an edge-enabled embedded platform. 
In this paper, a secure and energy efficient VLSI 
architecture is suggested to fill this gap with specific 
properties that may be provided to edge computing, 
which is the ACE architecture. The proposed design 
follows 
a 
Co-designing 
approach 
that 
includes 
lightweight hardware security primitives with energy

summarized as the following: 
1. 
An integrated safe and power efficient VLSI design 
optimized to the edge-enabled embedded system. 
2. 
Combinations of lightweight hardware security

3.

2. RELATED WORK 
There has been considerable research on low-power 
VLSI design methods to embedded platforms and 
system-on-chip (SoC) platforms. One of the best known 
and the most commonly used solutions to reduce the 
dynamic power is dynamic voltage and frequency 
scaling (DVFS) which changes the point at which the 
processors are operated according to the workload 
requirements [9], [10]. Clock gating methods and 
power gating techniques also decrease switching and 
leakage energy through disabling the functional units 
and power domains that are inactive, respectively 
[11], [12]. Besides, subthreshold and near-threshold 
computing have also been considered to provide very 
low energy operation in highly constrained embedded 
devices, but sacrificing performance and dramatically 
increasing variation [13]. Approximate computing is 
also a focus area as a solution to trade computational 
accuracy against energy efficiency in the error-
tolerant applications signal processing and machine 
learning at the edge [14]. In line with energy-efficient 
design, extensive literature has considered security of 
embedded systems by improving security using 
mechanism solving with the help of hardware. As part 
of the proposals to guard against firmware tampering, 
cloning, and unauthorized access, secure processor 
architectures with hardware roots of trust, secure 
boot chains and trusted execution environments (TEEs) 
have 
been 
suggested 
[5]-[7]. 
Cryptography 
accelerators with the lightweight have been designed 
and have been able to secure confidentiality and 
integrity features with lower latency than their 
software-based counterparts [8]. Nevertheless, most 
of such security-oriented designs impose significant 
area and power overhead making them less applicable 
in power-constrained edge devices [9]. Most recently, 
some studies have commenced research on how power 
management and security interact in embedded 
platforms. Secure processors and IoT oriented secure 
SoCs that operate energy awareness have been 
mentioned,with selective security features being 
enabled and disabled when needed depending on the 
application demands [2]. However, such solutions, in 
most cases, consider the power optimization and 
security as loosely loosely coupled entities rather than 
harmoniously designed to be co-architectural. Security 
mechanisms 
are 
often 
added 
as 
non-design 
considerations 
in 
many 
situations 
resulting 
in 
inefficient trade-offs between energy consumption, 
performance, and protection level. 
In general, current studies are deficient in a 
comprehensive VLSI design, which is jointly optimized 
energy and hardware-level security, at the initial 
design phases, especially when considering edge-
enabled embedded systems. This promptness is the 
inspiration of the proposed work that unites the 
lightweight security primitives with the multi-level 
power management in a single VLSI architecture that 
is viable in energy-constrained and security-sensitive 
edge computing applications. 
 
3. Methodology: Proposed Secure and Energy-
Optimized VLSI Architecture 
3.1 Design Objectives 
The proposed VLSI will support the high-performance 
aspects of edge-enabled embedded systems that used 
minimal amounts of energy, and may also be 
vulnerable to a variety of security dangers. The edge 
platforms usually have to handle the heterogeneous 
workloads whose computational needs vary over time

3.2 Architecture Overview 
The proposed secure and energy-optimized VLSI 
architecture is a modular system-on-chip (SoC), which 
is conceptually represented in Fig. 1 ( Physical-Level 
Schematic Representation of the Proposed Secure and 
Energy-Optimized 
VLSI 
Architecture 
). 
The 
architecture consists of a light embeddable processing 
core, on-chip instruction and data memory, peripheral 
interfaces, a specific security management unit (SMU) 
and an energy management controller (EMC). Such a 
modular structure allows functional blocks to be 
optimally controlled on an individual basis and also 
allows flexibility in integration between the various 
edge applications. As demonstrated in Fig. 1, the 
processing core is used to develop application 
workloads and it also interacts with the memory 
subsystem via low-latency interconnect to provide 
efficient access and execution of data. The security 
management unit works in tandem with the core and 
aims at ensuring trusted execution environment is 
established. It incorporates a hardware root of trust, 
safety boot logic as well as a slim cryptographic 
accelerator. The secure boot logic can ensure the 
integrity and authenticity of firmware images during 
system start-up and verify the authenticity of the 
firmware images prior to execution, eliminating the 
unauthorized execution of codes and tampering of 
firmware. The energy management controller is using 
constantly varied workload properties, including 
instruction activity and which modules are in use and 
dynamically adjusts the power states over the 
architecture. The proposed architecture can prioritize 
awareness of the security state by tightly integrating 
power management with security operations, as shown 
in Fig. 1, to ensure the unnecessary power overhead 
resulting security operations is eliminated and, as 
such, is well suited to energy-constrained and 
security-critical edge-based embedded systems.

3.4 Hardware Security Integration 
Security is not considered as an application-level or 
software addition to the proposed architecture, but 
rather, it is encompassed in the hardware mechanism 
as a dedicated mechanism as shown in Fig. 3. 
Hardware root of trust Hardware root of trust provides 
a secure foundation over which critical cryptographic 
information is stored and authenticated to prevent 
unauthorized access to and physical attacks. At system 
booting, the secure boot system verifies firmware 
images through a hash-based integrity check and a 
digital signature by using algorithms on cryptographic 
processes. Firmware with passing authentication is 
positively engaged thus preventing cloning and 
firmware 
tampering 
attacks. 
The 
cryptographic 
acceleration is also incorporated with lightweight 
tending in order to facilitate encryption and hashing 
algorithms needed to enable safe communication and 
securing the safety of the data. The hardware-based 
cryptography is much faster in the execution time and 
energy usage than software-only implementation. The 
given design provides a reasonable trade-off between 
the 
intensity 
of 
protection 
and 
the 
energy 
consumption through designing the major facilities of 
security and power management closely related to the 
architecture. It is a co-design method which ensures 
that security operations are conducted when needed, 
and at the correct power levels, thus the architecture 
is highly suitable in energy-constrained security-
intensive edge-enabled embedded systems.

4. Methodology: Hardware Implementation and 
Evaluation Setup 
4.1 RTL Design and Implementation Flow 
Its implemented secure and power-efficient VLSI 
architecture is now done with a register-transfer level 
(RTL) design methodology so that precise control can 
be exercised on architecture features, timing behavior 
and power management mechanisms. All of the 
functional 
modules 
(processing 
core, 
security 
management unit, and energy management controller) 
are described in a hardware description language, and 
incorporated into a modular system-on-chip (SoC) 
environment. This modular RTL architecture allows the 
guarantee of the verification and optimization of 
components, at the same time preserving the system 
coherence. The RTL design is based on a common 
digital 
design 
cycle 
that 
includes 
functional 
simulation, 
logic 
synthesis 
and 
post-synthesis 
verification. The first step is to make sure that 
functional correctness is achieved by simulating 
(cyclically) with representative edge workloads to 
verify the proper interaction of computation, power 
management and security. The design is then 
synthesized with electronic design automation (EDA) 
tools using industry standard electronics technology 
nodes. The specification of timing constraints is to 
indicate realistic operating environment of edge-
enabled embedded systems.

4.4 Scalability and Technology Portability 
To test scalability, the proposed architecture is tested 
with various workloads levels and operating conditions 
as edge computing applications are dynamic in nature. 
The modular RTL architecture enables to adapt easily 
to the various application needs and technology nodes 
without 
architecture-based 
modification. 
This

architecture to be implemented on a large variety of

edge intelligence platforms. 
On the whole, the evaluation procedure and hardware

6. DISCUSSION 
The findings validate that system-level optimization in 
terms of energy efficiency and hardware security is 
not only possible, but also extremely useful towards 
edge-enabled embedded systems. In contrast to the 
traditional designs, where the security functions are 
incorporated as after-design features, the co-design 
approach proposed helps to reduce the redundant 
energy use and overhead in areas. Unlike other 
existing energy-efficient embedded architectures, 
which put the primary emphasis on DVFS and clock 
gating, the proposed design provides an extra benefit 
of implementing security-aware energy reduction. In 
the 
same 
manner, 
the 
proposed 
architecture 
demonstrates that the lightweight hardware security 
primitives can be implemented with a low overhead, 
as compared to secure processor designs, which 
apportion a significant overhead in terms of both 
power 
consumption 
and 
area 
demands. 
The 
performance degradation seen with intense safe boot 
and cryptographic tasks suggests that hardware-
supported security measures are better than software-
based solutions to edge systems, especially where 
latency- and energy-critical applications are used. 
Also, the modularity of the architecture can be scaled 
and extended in the future including trusted execution 
environments, AI accelerators or domain specific 
processing units. 
On 
the 
whole, 
the 
discussion 
indicates 
that 
architectural 
design 
co-optimization 
of 
power 
operation and security is one of the potential trends 
that next-generation edge computing hardware can 
follow. The offered architecture incorporates a 
significant disparity in current research as it provides 
energy-efficient functioning and powerful security in a 
single VLSI system.

7. Security Analysis 
To consider the merit of the suggested secure and 
energy-saving VLSI architecture, extensive security 
analysis is provided with the emphasis on a realistic 
threat model that is relevant to the embedded systems 
with edges. Edge devices tend to be arranged in low-
security physical locations with network connectivity 
which makes them vulnerable to both local and 
remote attacks. Thus the threat model assumes 
adversaries who have the ability to tamper with 
firmware, gain unauthorized privileges and access, 
clone, have limited physical invasive power and 
attacks based on communications. 
The security boot mechanism is provided as a 
safeguard against the integrity of firmware and 
implemented within the security management unit. 
Cryptographic verification of firmware images during 
system startup is done by checking hash-based 
integrity checks and digital signature based on the 
hardware root of trust. Authenticated firmware is 
authorized to be executed and this effectively 
prevents the malicious injections of the code, 
replacing firmware and duplicating the device. This is 
an assurance of sealed bootchain both during the 
power-up and during the runtime execution. 
The defenses against unauthorized access to sensitive 
data and cryptographic keys are the hardware root of 
trust, to offer a safe storage and authentication 
anchor, not connected to the core processor. The keys 
and security credentials are stored in non- volatile 
memory area or in secure hardware registers that do 
not allow unprivileged software to access, hence 
limiting the attack surface accessible to the software-
based exploits. 
The lightweight cryptographic accelerator supports the 
secure data transmission and facilitates hardware-
based encryption and hashing. The architecture avoids 
cryptographic processing the software stack with 
ensuring confidentiality and data integrity over 
communication 
with 
external 
devices 
or 
edge 
gateways by lowering the execution latency as well as 
reducing energy expenditure. Hardware cryptography 
is also more resistant to timing attacks than software 
only. 
Although the explicit countermeasures against the 
advanced side-channel attack, such as the use of 
different power analysis algorithm or electromagnetic 
analysis algorithm are not explicitly integrated into 
the current architecture, the integrated power 
management 
measures 
minimize 
the 
observable 
difference in power consumption at the normal 
operation. In addition, the modular architecture of 
security management unit allows extension in the 
future such as cores with side-channel resistance to 
cryptography and anomaly monitoring during running. 
In general, it can be seen that the analysis of its 
security shows that the proposed architecture has high 
resistance to most threats that are typical of 
firmware-based, access-based, and communication-
based of the threat. Co-designing security and power 
management provides a scalable infrastructure of 
deploying trusted and energy-sensitive edge-enabled 
embedded systems. 
 
CONCLUSION 
In this paper, a secure and energy-optimized VLSI 
architecture specific to edge-enabled embedded 
systems that are subject to strict power and security 
specifications was introduced. The solution has 
considered lightweight hardware security mechanisms 
alongside multi-level energy optimization techniques 
by using a co-design paradigm, which has resulted in 
efficient and reliable edge computing platforms. The 
most extensive contributions of this work consists in 
the design of a modular system-on-chip architecture 
which integrates a hardware root of trust, secure boot 
mode 
along 
with 
lightweight 
cryptographic 
acceleration with dynamic voltage and frequency 
scaling, fine-grained clock gating, and power gating. 
The results of post-synthesis evaluation indicate that 
the designed architecture is capable of obtaining high 
power consumption and energy per operation and also 
introduces a relatively small silicon area overhead. 
Their findings confirm that it is possible to achieve 
hardware-inspired security and aggressive power 
optimization through the conjunction of the necessary 
performance without sacrificing the security and 
energy cost making the architecture ideally suited to 
the needs of energy-limited and security-conscious 
edge 
applications.

than 
the 
short-term 
outcomes, this work provides a step of scaling to be 
used in the future. Future research avenues are the 
combination 
of 
enhanced 
trusted 
execution 
environments, side-channel resistant cryptographic 
cores, and runtime security checking scams. Moreover, 
the architecture can also be scaled to provide domain-
specific accelerators, e.g., artificial intelligence and 
machine learning inference engines, to address the 
increasing computing requirements of next-generation 
edge intelligence applications. Future employment can 
also focus on adaptive protection policies, which may 
be able to balance the strength of protection and the 
consumption of power depending on the application 
context. In general, the suggested hardened and 
energy-efficient VLSI design provides a realistic and 
scalable solution to the energy consumption issues and 
security problems facing edge-enabled embedded 
systems, and presents both helpful information to the 
design of next-generation low-power and trustful 
architecture.

Abstract: Embedded systems with edges are critical in the new applications in the Internet of Things (IoT), smart healthcare, industrial automation and, cyber physical infrastructures. Such systems need to be under strict energy requirements and, at the same time, be highly resistant to tampering with their firmwares, unauthorized access, and physical attacks. Nevertheless, the majority of VLSI architectures have methods to discuss energy efficiency and security as orthogonal design constraints, resulting in inefficient trade-offs and higher overheads when implemented in resource-constrained edge conditions. The current paper suggests a safe and power efficient VLSI design that is directly aimed at edge-driven embedded systems. This proposal follows the principle of unified co-design that can be utilized to integrate lightweight hardware security primitives such as a hardware root of trust, secure boot mechanism, cryptographic acceleration with multi-level energy optimization methods, such as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), fine-grained clock gating, and power gating. A design methodology based on register-transfer level (RTL) is used to describe the architecture and it is implemented in industry-standard synthesis tools to make it practically feasible. A detailed analysis of the proposed design with realistic edge workloads proves that the design significantly reduces the overall energy consumption and the energy per operation relative to a nominal embedded architecture with only a low overhead in the area and performance. Moreover, the internal security provisions offer a high level of protection against high firmware-based and communication threats without negating energy high efficiency. The findings validate that security and power co-optimization in architectural settings is an effective and required process of the next-generation edge computing platforms. The proposed VLSI architecture will come up with a secure, scalable, and low-energy solution to low-latency and low-power edge intelligence applications. Power-efficient architectures do not put security into consideration and secure processor designs often provide high overheads of area and energy [7], [8] because protection mechanisms are added to them. Also, numerous security mechanisms are often added as post-design additions instead of being co-designed with power management, and it results in an inefficient trade-off into the aptness of resource-constrained edge environments. This points at a critical research void, namely the absence of an integrated VLSI architecture that becomes optimized in terms of energy efficiency and hardware-level security of an edge-enabled embedded platform. In this paper, a secure and energy efficient VLSI architecture is suggested to fill this gap with specific properties that may be provided to edge computing, which is the ACE architecture. The proposed design follows a Co-designing approach that includes lightweight hardware security primitives with energy optimization at the multiple level with at the architectural level.
